(b) Normal clause: re-derived (V_1+V_2) - theta = (2+SR^2) - 2(1-rho) - SR^2(1-rho^2) = rho(2 + SR^2 rho); for SR^2 < 2 the factor is at least 2 - SR^2 > 0, so the sign is rho's. Numerically (scratchpad scripts/prop54.py) the identity holds at 10 (SR, rho) pairs, and asymptotic sizes are 0.0056 (SR 0.1, rho 0.5; Monte Carlo 0.0067, T = 1500, 3000 reps), 0.1091 (0.1, -0.5; MC 0.1107), 0.0246 (SR 2, rho -0.9; MC 0.0227, undersized, so the SR^2 < 2 condition is needed) and exactly 0.0500 (SR 2, rho -0.5, where 2 + SR^2 rho = 0). Re-derived the proposition myself: for jointly normal returns psi_i = u_i - (SR_i/2) He2(u_i) with He2(u) = u^2 - 1, and Cov(u_1, u_2) = rho, Cov(He2(u_1), He2(u_2)) = 2 rho^2, cross terms between He1 and He2 vanish, so Var psi_i = 1 + SR_i^2/2 and Cov(psi_1, psi_2) = rho + SR_1 SR_2 rho^2/2; hence theta = Var(psi_1 - psi_2) = 2(1 - rho) + (SR_1^2 + SR_2^2)/2 - SR_1 SR_2 rho^2, which is the page's (5). With SR_1 = SR_2 = SR: (V_1 + V_2) - theta = rho (2 + SR^2 rho) (identity checked at 1000 random (SR, rho), max error 2.7e-15, scratchpad verify11-L07-L08/scripts/prop54.py). For SR^2 < 2 the factor 2 + SR^2 rho >= 2 - SR^2 > 0 on [-1, 1], so (V_1 + V_2) - theta has the sign of rho: theta < V_1 + V_2 (naive test undersized) for rho > 0 and theta > V_1 + V_2 (oversized) for rho < 0; a grid of 200 values of SR^2 in [0, 1.999] x 401 values of rho found 0 sign violations. The condition is sharp: SR = 2, rho = -0.9 gives (V_1+V_2)/theta = 1.316 and asymptotic naive size 0.0246 < 0.05 under negative correlation, so the round-9 text (an unconditional 'sign of the correlation') was false and the new text is exactly as strong as Proposition 5.4: it says that the direction is what the proposition gives, and the sign rule only for normal returns, a common Sharpe ratio and SR^2 < 2. Reading of 'normal returns': Proposition 5.4's proof reaches the sign rule through (5), the iid bivariate-normal case of Corollary 5.2, so 'normal returns' means jointly normal returns. Marginal normality alone would not fix the sign (u_2 = eps u_1 with eps = +-1 independent of u_1 and mean rho has N(0,1) margins and correlation rho, but kappa_12 = kappa_21 = 0, kappa_22 = 3 and theta = 2 - 2 rho, so (V_1+V_2) - theta = SR^2 + 2 rho > 0 at rho = -0.01, SR^2 = 0.1). The phrase is the proposition's own shorthand, which rounds 7-9 accepted and which the quiz item now spells out ('jointly normal'); saying 'jointly normal' in Proposition 5.4, Remark 5.6, Misconception 6, the key-results row and card S7-c158 would remove the ambiguity: optional hardening, not a failure. The rest of the Remark re-read against its sources: statistic max_k sqrt(T)(SR-hat_k - SR-hat_0) and 'one stationary-bootstrap index sequence for the benchmark and all strategies together' = L04 Problem R1 (read in L04.html); the Diebold-Mariano construction = L04 Definition 1.2 (Bartlett long-run variance); 'independent resampling ... overstates the multiplicity and throws away power' = L05 Section 4 (read in L05.html); theta = Var(psi_1 - psi_2) = Theorem 5.1; the T span (Ledoit and Wolf keep the delta-method gradient and replace the iid covariance by its long-run covariance, HAC kernel) = Sections 3 and 3.1 of IEW Working Paper 320, January 2008, which I downloaded again (econ.uzh.ch/apps/workingpapers/wp/iewwp320.pdf): (3) sqrt(T)(v-hat - v) -> N(0, Psi), (4)-(5) delta method with standard error from Psi-hat, 3.1 'HAC Inference' with Psi the limit of the autocovariance sums and a kernel estimator Psi-hat; linearizing their gradient gives psi_1 - psi_2 exactly (Theorem 5.1 Step 3). All links in the paragraph resolve (scratchpad verify11-L07-L08/scripts/xrefs.py, check_pages PASS).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Misconception 6 ('Two Sharpe ratios whose separate confidence intervals overlap cannot be told apart'), last sentence: 'For normal returns with a common per-period Sharpe ratio whose square is below 2, the error runs the other way under negative correlation: the naive test rejects a true null too often (Proposition 5.4, Lab 4).'
rows.evidence: Round-9 FAIL re-checked from scratch. The hunk (line 570) replaces 'With negatively correlated strategies the error runs the other way:' by 'For normal returns with a common per-period Sharpe ratio whose square is below 2, the error runs the other way under negative correlation:' and nothing else. Under those conditions (V_1 + V_2) - theta = rho (2 + SR^2 rho) < 0 for every rho in [-1, 0) (derivation in L07-math-remark5.6), so theta > V_1 + V_2 and the naive test is oversized: asymptotic size 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt((V_1+V_2)/theta))) = 0.1094 at rho = -0.5 and 0.1548 at rho = -0.9 with SR = 0.05 (scratchpad verify11-L07-L08/scripts/prop54.py). The sentence cites Lab 4, which supports it: my run of the twin (and the page's expected block, byte-identical) shows the naive rejection rate 0.1175 at rho = -0.5 in 4000 jointly normal samples with both daily Sharpe ratios 0.05, against 0.0498 at rho = 0 and 0.0057 at rho = 0.5. 'Per-period' is the scale on which the proposition states SR^2 < 2 and matches the lesson's convention (Definition 1.1 defines SR = mu/sigma per period; Example 5.5 labels annualized values as annualized); an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.5 has per-period square 0.009, so a reader who read the condition on the annualized scale would be wrongly alarmed, which the word 'per-period' prevents. The old sentence was wrong for non-normal returns and for SR^2 > 2 (SR = 2, rho = -0.9: size 0.0246, undersized); the new one is not. The first part of the paragraph is unchanged and rechecked (Example 5.5: theta-hat = 0.100434, se = 0.008932, Z = 2.239, two-sided p = 0.0251; naive 2.0026, se 0.039883, Z = 0.501, p = 0.616; se ratio 4.465 ('4.5 times'); single annualized se sqrt(252 x 1.0018/1259) = 0.4478 ('about 0.45'); annualized difference 0.02 sqrt(252) = 0.3175 ('0.32')). The sentence stays inside the Misconception's point and no longer overreaches. Same optional note on 'normal returns' = jointly normal as in L07-math-remark5.6.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html quiz item 15 (stem 'Two strategies with jointly normal returns have correlation 0.9 and equal true per-period Sharpe ratios. A test of equal Sharpe ratios that treats them as independent, at nominal level 5%, rejects...') and its explanation 'Proposition 5.4 for normal returns: the naive variance V_1 + V_2 is about 10 times theta at rho = 0.9 and a Sharpe ratio near zero, so the statistic is far too small. Lab 4: no rejections in 4000 samples.'
rows.evidence: Round-9 FAIL re-checked from scratch. Hunks (lines 872 and 878): the stem gains 'with jointly normal returns' and 'per-period' (and loses the singular 'return'), the explanation gains 'for normal returns' and 'and a Sharpe ratio near zero'; options unchanged ('about 5% of the time', 'almost never' [data-correct], 'far more than 5% of the time'). Recomputed (scratchpad verify11-L07-L08/scripts/prop54.py): for jointly normal returns with equal Sharpe ratios the ratio (V_1+V_2)/theta = (2 + SR^2)/(2(1 - rho) + SR^2 (1 - rho^2)) is 10.000 at SR = 0, 9.989 at SR = 0.05 (the lab's value), 7.69 at SR = 1 and tends to 5.265 as SR grows (minimum over SR in [0, 50] 5.265); the asymptotic rejection probability 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(ratio))) is 5.7e-10 at SR = 0, 5.8e-10 at SR = 0.05, 5.5e-8 at SR = 1 and at most 6.9e-6 at SR = 50. So 'almost never' is true for every common per-period Sharpe ratio under joint normality, the stem needs no 'near zero', and the explanation's 'about 10 times' is correct where it is stated (Sharpe ratio near zero). 'About 5%' and 'far more than 5%' are false at rho = 0.9. The explanation's 'Lab 4: no rejections in 4000 samples' = expected-block row '0.9 0.0517 0.0000' (page = twin = my run). iid over time is the lesson's standing assumption (Theorem 5.1) and, like the other quiz items (q12 'normal daily returns', q14 'true Sharpe ratio and moments are known'), the item does not restate it; exactly one option carries data-correct; the item has an explanation. The fix of round 9 is complete and introduces no neighbouring error.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html Lab 4 code: halves() and pbo_fast() (lines 496-531); tests/labs/S7/lab-S7-L08-4.py

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html #canon-breaks closing paragraph 'Biased returns pass through every correction in this module.' (line 591)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 3dd9a69 (git diff checked); round-9 evidence: Re-derived. Setup: recorded returns have limiting Sharpe ratio SR_n + delta_n, delta_n > 0, where SR_n is the investable one. (i) A constant cost k per period omitted from returns of volatility sigma_n: recorded mean = true mean + k, volatility unchanged, so the recorded Sharpe ratio is SR_n + k/sigma_n, delta_n = k/sigma_n, independent of T: correct. (ii) The luck hurdle (2) of Lesson 1 is sqrt(2 ln N / T) per period (Corollary 2.2, checked in L01.html) and the one-sided Bonferroni hurdle on a per-period Sharpe ratio is Phi^-1(1 - alpha/N)/sqrt(T) (Lesson 2's critical value Phi^-1(1 - alpha/m) for the z-statistic sqrt(T) SR-hat, whose null variance is 1/T by Lesson 1): both are constant multiples of 1/sqrt(T) at fixed N and alpha. (iii) With SR_n = 0 the estimate converges in probability to delta_n > 0 (law of large numbers for the sample mean and variance) while either hurdle tends to 0, so the probability of clearing it tends to 1 for every fixed N; the z-statistic sqrt(T) SR-hat is about sqrt(T) delta_n, which exceeds any fixed critical value eventually. 'A longer history makes the false backtest look more convincing' follows. (iv) N = 1: Bonferroni threshold alpha/1, Holm's first step alpha/(m+1-1) = alpha, and Benjamini-Hochberg's threshold alpha x 1/1 are all the uncorrected level alpha: correct. Simulation (scratchpad scripts/biased_sim.py; normal returns, monthly sigma 4%, omitted cost 0.1% per month so delta = 0.025, N = 20, alpha = 0.05, 4000 samples each): the probability that a zero-skill trial clears the Bonferroni hurdle rises with T from 0.005 (T = 60) to 0.020 (960), 0.108 (3840) and 0.273 (7680), and the luck hurdle from 0.013 to 0.404, mean estimate 0.025 throughout, slowly but monotonically towards 1 as the sqrt(T) delta_n argument predicts (the page claims the limit, not a rate). Scope: the paragraph's claims are about the corrections' dependence on N and T, which is what is derived; it does not claim a size for any finite T. Notation: delta_n, k, sigma_n are used only inside this paragraph and are not registered symbols (notation.json read: no collision; delta also appears elsewhere in L08 as a standardized edge, local to those problems).
